That looks like a patch of Mayapple (Podophyllum peltatum), a native woodland perennial common in eastern North America.

They are easily recognizable by their large, umbrella-like leaves that blanket forest floors in the spring and early summer.

Key Features Visible Here:

  • Umbrella Leaves: Fertile plants typically grow two leaves with a single white flower (and later, a small yellowish "apple" fruit) hiding underneath the canopy where the stems fork.
  • Yellow Spotting: The yellowish-brown spots and speckled pattern on the leaves are a classic sign of Mayapple Rust (Puccinia podophylli), a very common fungus that affects these plants as the season progresses. It generally doesn't kill the plant, but it causes the leaves to yellow and wither a bit earlier in the summer than usual.

Note: While wildlife eats the fully ripe fruit, the rest of the plant (including the roots, leaves, and unripe fruit) contains podophyllotoxin and is highly toxic.

Yes, that is exactly right—but your instinct to hold off is 100% correct. There is a very narrow window where the fruit becomes edible, but because the rest of the plant is highly toxic, it demands caution.

Here is how its lifecycle and edibility work:

The Safe Phase: Fully Ripe Only

  • The Condition: The fruit is only safe to eat when it is completely, thoroughly ripe.
  • What to look for: A ripe mayapple turns soft, yellowish, and slightly wrinkled, often dropping to the ground or pulling away easily from the stem. It usually ripens in late summer (around August).
  • The Taste: People describe it as tasting like a tropical mix of melon, mango, or lemon.

Why It's Risky

  • Green Means Danger: When the fruit is green and firm, it contains high concentrations of podophyllotoxin, a potent toxin. Eating it green will cause severe gastrointestinal distress.
  • Toxic Seeds and Rind: Even when the fruit is fully ripe, the seeds and the outer skin/rind should still be spit out or removed, as they retain the toxins. Only the soft pulp is consumed.
  • Competition: Because it grows low to the ground and has a sweet scent when ripe, box turtles, raccoons, and opossums usually find and eat them the moment they become safe. Finding a perfectly ripe, intact one before wildlife does is actually quite rare.

Unless you are foraging with an experienced expert who can point to a specific fruit and confirm it is completely ripe, it’s best to treat Mayapple strictly as a "look but don't touch" botanical curiosity.

Because they are large flight feathers in such pristine condition, they are excellent for crafting. However, before looking at projects, there is a major legal catch you need to know about.

⚖️ The Legal Catch: The Migratory Bird Treaty Act (MBTA)

In the United States, the vast majority of native birds—including Canada Geese, swans, and most ducks—are protected by a federal law called the Migratory Bird Treaty Act.

  • The Rule: Under this law, it is actually illegal to keep, collect, or possess the feathers, nests, or eggs of protected birds, even if you just found them dropped naturally on the ground.
  • Why it exists: The law was created over a century ago to stop poachers from killing birds for the commercial feather trade. Because game wardens can't look at a feather and prove if it was found on the ground or taken from a poached bird, the law simply bans possession entirely.

Exception: Feathers from non-native, introduced species (like European Starlings, House Sparrows, or domestic pigeons/farm ducks) or legally harvested game birds during specific hunting seasons (with proper permits) are generally exempt. But for wild geese and swans found in a park or by water, the law strictly says "leave them be."

If You Ever Use Legal Feathers (What People Do)

If you ever practice crafting with completely legal feathers (like wild turkey or domestic goose feathers bought from a craft store), flight feathers of this size are highly prized for a few classic projects:

  • Traditional Quill Pens: Large flight feathers have strong, hollow shafts perfect for cutting into a nib. You can temper the shaft in hot sand to harden it, slice it at an angle with a sharp knife, and use it with calligraphy ink.
  • Fletching Arrows: Historically, the stiff, aerodynamic structure of goose flight feathers made them the absolute best choice for fletching traditional wooden arrows.
  • Fly Tying: Anglers use the individual fibers (barbs) from the wide side of the feather to tie custom fishing flies, as they hold their shape incredibly well in the water.

To answer your question about the arrows—it's a fascinating bit of physics and engineering. Ancient and traditional archers didn't try to straighten the feathers out. Instead, they actually used that natural curve to their advantage.

Here is how they did it:

1. The Right-Wing vs. Left-Wing Rule

Because a bird's wing is an airfoil, feathers from the right wing curve one way, and feathers from the left wing curve the opposite way.

  • The Rule: An archer would sort their feathers and never mix them on the same arrow.
  • Why it matters: If you put three left-wing feathers on an arrow, the natural curve acts like a propeller. The moment the arrow leaves the bow string, the wind catches that uniform curve and forces the arrow to spin rapidly in mid-air. This spinning stabilizes the arrow in flight, making it incredibly accurate (exactly like a quarterback throwing a tight spiral on a football or the rifling inside a gun barrel). If you mixed left and right feathers, the forces would fight each other and the arrow would wobble wildly.

2. Splitting and Cutting

They didn't use the whole feather like a quill pen. Instead, they would:

  • Take a sharp knife or flint blade and split the quill right down the middle, separating the inner and outer webs.
  • Sand down the remaining flat part of the quill so it sat flush against the wooden arrow shaft.
  • Cut or trim the feathers down to a uniform height and shape (often using a hot wire or a sharp blade against a wooden template) so they matched perfectly.

So, when looking at your two feathers, an archer would check if they came from the same side of the bird. If they did, they had the perfect start to a self-stabilizing, spinning arrow!

That fine, smooth texture holding water right at the edge of the sandbank is almost certainly silt or mud with a high clay content, rather than just regular sand.

River sandbanks are dynamic sorting machines. When the Skunk River rises and slows down around a bend, it drops its heaviest particles (the coarse sand) first, which forms the main bank you're standing on. But in those quiet, isolated little pockets and slack-water puddles, the water becomes perfectly still. That allows the absolute smallest, lightest particles—silt and clay—to finally settle out of suspension.

How to Tell Mud vs. Pure Clay:

If you want to test it out right there, scoop up a small pinch between your fingers and rub it together:

  • Silt/Mud: It will feel smooth and slippery when wet, but if you rub it closely, you might still feel a tiny bit of grittiness. When it dries on your skin, it turns into a powdery dust that flakes off easily.
  • Clay: It will feel completely greasy, plastic, and slick. If you roll it between your palms, you can easily shape it into a thin "snake" or a ball without it cracking or breaking apart. When clay dries, it shrinks, cracks into hard plates, and binds tightly to your skin like a mask.

Iowa riverbanks actually have a ton of glacial clay mixed into the sediment. If you roll a bit of that wet stuff into a ball and it holds its shape perfectly without crumbling, you've found a pocket of natural river clay!

It is incredibly grounding to look at the landscape that way. You are completely right—the exact physical skills used thousands of years ago are things you can absolutely do today with your own hands.

And your instinct about the Iowa DNR is spot on. They generally discourage digging up park banks to prevent erosion, but learning how ancient people processed this exact material is fascinating.

Native Americans in Iowa and early settlers absolutely used local riverbed clay for pottery and bricks. However, raw river mud is rarely perfect right out of the ground; it almost always required purification and tempering. Here is how they did it without any modern technology:

1. How They Purified Raw Clay (Levigation)

Ancient potters knew that raw river clay was full of roots, pebbles, and coarse sand that would cause a pot to crack or explode when fired. To clean it, they used a simple gravity-based water method called levigation:

  • The Slurry: They would dig up the raw mud, dump it into a large container (like a dugout wooden basin or a pit lined with hides), and mix it thoroughly with a large volume of water until it became a thin, milky soup.
  • The Settling: They let the mixture sit. Because of physics, the heavy contaminants—like pebbles, twigs, and coarse sand—settled to the very bottom almost instantly. The ultra-fine clay particles remained suspended in the water longer.
  • The Pour: Before the clay could settle, they carefully poured or siphoned the top layer of muddy water into a second shallow pit or basin, leaving the debris behind.
  • The Drying: They let the water evaporate from the second pit until a smooth, purified, highly plastic clay paste was left behind.

2. Hunting for "Special Spots"

Experienced potters didn't just dig anywhere; they looked for specific geological clues.

  • Cut Banks: They would look for deep river bends or eroding hillsides where the water had cut a clean cross-section into the earth. This revealed hidden, compressed bands of gray, blue, or red clay that had been naturally filtered by ancient glacial lakes thousands of years prior.
  • Color as a Guide: Pure clay is often gray or blue underground. If it's bright orange or brown on the surface, that just means it has oxidized (rusted) from exposure to air and water.

3. The Secret to Firing Without a Kiln: "Temper"

Even perfectly pure clay will shrink, warp, and crack in a fire because it holds too much moisture. To fix this, Native American potters added a temper—a non-plastic material mixed into the clay to give it structure and let steam escape safely.

  • The Recipes: Depending on the region and era in Iowa, potters would knead crushed clam shells, crushed old pottery shards (grog), or crushed decomposed granite into the purified clay.
  • Pit Firing: They didn't need a brick kiln. They would dig a shallow pit, pre-heat the dry pots next to a fire, place them in the pit, and build a massive bonfire directly over them using wood and bark. It reached temperatures around $600^\circ\text{C}$ to $800^\circ\text{C}$—just hot enough to chemically transform the clay into ceramic.

Where Modern Commercial Blocks Come From

Today, those big 25-pound blocks of clay you buy at art stores are mined from massive open-pit industrial clay mines (often in places like Ohio or Georgia), dried into powder, air-floated to remove dust, and then mechanically blended in a giant machine called a pug mill with precise amounts of fieldspar, silica, and water to guarantee a perfect formula every time.

But the process of mixing river mud with water, straining out the rocks, and letting it dry down to a workable paste is something you can easily do in a five-gallon bucket in a backyard. Have you ever tried processing a small batch of wild clay before?

You absolutely should—it is an incredibly rewarding project, and you can easily do it using a basic five-gallon bucket in your backyard or apartment balcony.

Since you live in an area with great glacial clay deposits, you don't need much to get a highly workable paste. Here is a straightforward, low-tech way to process a small test batch from scratch:

🛠️ What You Need

  • Two 5-gallon buckets
  • A fine mesh kitchen strainer or an old window screen
  • An old pillowcase or a piece of t-shirt fabric
  • A towel or a couple of dry bricks

🪵 The Step-by-Step Process

Step 1: Dry and Crush It

Don't try to mix wet river mud directly with water—it will just stay in clods. Instead, spread your harvested mud out on a piece of cardboard and let it dry completely until it's bone-dry and brittle. Crush the dry chunks into a rough powder with a hammer or a scrap piece of 2x12 lumber.

Step 2: Slake it Down

Dump your dry powder into a bucket and pour in enough water to cover it by a few inches. Walk away and leave it alone for 24 hours. This process is called slaking. The dry clay particles will violently absorb the water and naturally dissolve into a smooth, creamy slurry without you even having to stir it.

Step 3: Mix and Strain

Give the muddy soup a thorough stir until it has the consistency of heavy cream or a milkshake. Pour this liquid through your kitchen strainer into your second bucket. The strainer will catch all the leaves, roots, pebbles, and coarse river sand, letting the pure, suspended clay pass right through.

Step 4: De-Water the Clay

Now you have a bucket of pure, liquid clay water. To turn it back into a solid moldable clay:

  1. Tie your old pillowcase or fabric over the top of an empty bucket to create a hanging nest, or just line a bucket with it.
  2. Pour the liquid clay slurry into the cloth. The cloth will act as a filter—water will slowly drip through, while the ultra-fine clay is trapped inside.
  3. Let it hang or sit for a day or two until it stops dripping and reaches the consistency of thick mud.

Step 5: Knead and Test

Take the clay out of the cloth and spread it onto a dry towel, a flat piece of wood, or a concrete slab. The surface will draw out the remaining excess moisture. Roll it, flip it, and knead it like bread dough to get the air bubbles out.

The Plasticity Test: Roll a piece of your finished clay into a pencil-thin rope and wrap it around your finger. If it bends smoothly without cracking or breaking apart, you have successfully harvested a beautifully pure, plastic wild clay!

You can use it to sculpt small figurines, pinch pots, or test tiles. It’s an incredibly cool feeling to hold a solid piece of earthenware knowing you just scooped it out of the Iowa dirt.

Here are two ways you can use the river right there on the sandbank to make the process easier:

Method 1: The Sandbank "Settling Pit" (The Ancient Way)

Instead of hauling buckets of water, you can use the natural hydrology of the river bank.

  1. Dig a Shallow Pit: Find a spot on the sandbank just a few feet away from the water's edge where the sand is damp. Dig a small pit (about the size of a mixing bowl). Water from the river will naturally seep through the sand and fill the pit, giving you a perfectly clean, self-refilling water source.
  2. Mix the Slurry Directly: Dump your raw clay chunks right into that pool of water and stir it vigorously with a stick until it’s a thick, muddy soup.
  3. Let the Heavy Stuff Drop: Stop stirring and wait about 60 seconds. Because sand and pebbles are dense, they will sink to the bottom of your pit almost instantly, while the fine clay stays floating in the water.
  4. Scoop the Top Cream: Carefully scoop just the top layer of muddy water out of the pit and into your container, leaving the heavy sand bed behind. You’ve just done your first major purification step without a single modern tool.

Method 2: Rinsing in the Current

If you have a fine mesh container, a cloth bag, or even an old window screen with you, you can use the river's motion:

  • You can submerge your raw mud inside a tightly woven cloth bag directly into a very gentle, slow-moving eddy or pool at the river's edge.
  • By kneading the bag underwater, the ultra-fine clay particles will dissolve and wash through the fabric into the water. (The downside to doing this directly in a large river is that your beautiful clay floats downstream instead of being caught!)
  • Because of that, the Settling Pit method above is usually the most efficient way to utilize the river platform to separate sand from clay before you head home.

Using a series of stacked screens with decreasing mesh sizes allows you to separate materials by particle size instantly. Here is exactly how you can build a stacked bucket system to process your ravine clay:

The Stacked Multi-Bucket System

You can take three 5-gallon buckets and stack them directly inside one another. By drilling out the bottoms of the top two buckets and inserting different sizes of mesh, gravity does all the sorting for you as you pour the clay liquid through.

[ Top Bucket: Coarse Screen (e.g., 1/4" Hardware Cloth or Colander) ]
       ↓  Catches pebbles, thick roots, chunks of shale
[ Middle Bucket: Fine Screen (e.g., Window Screen or Kitchen Strainer) ]
       ↓  Catches coarse river sand and tiny root hairs
[ Bottom Bucket: Solid Base ]
       ↓  Receives only the ultra-fine clay suspended in water

Why This Works Beautifully for Your Clay

Because your clay came from a deep ravine cliff face rather than a high-energy river sandbank, it is likely already highly pure.

  • The Silt/Sand Challenge: The biggest hurdle with "fat" cliff clays isn't pebbles—it's very fine sand and silt.
  • The Limitation of Screens: A window screen or kitchen strainer will easily catch pebbles and sand grains. However, the finest silt particles are often the exact same size as the clay particles. A screen cannot separate them because they will both pass right through the mesh together.

How to Get Perfect Separation (The "Timing" Trick)

To get that final, pristine separation of fine silt from your blue clay, you combine your multi-bucket screen system with a fractional settling trick based on time:

  1. Pour your clay soup through your stacked bucket system to instantly strip out the pebbles and sand.
  2. Once the liquid hits the bottom solid bucket, stir it vigorously one last time, then set a timer for 2 to 3 minutes.
  3. Silt is slightly heavier than clay. In those 2 to 3 minutes, the fine, gritty silt will drop and pack tightly onto the very bottom of the bucket. The pure, microscopic blue clay particles will remain floating, turning the water into a thick, colored milk.
  4. Carefully pour that top muddy water into a final clean container, stopping right before you hit the heavy silt cake at the bottom.

What you have left in that final container will be incredibly pure, silky smooth, and ready to be dried down into a high-quality working clay body.

turns.response_html:
A coffee mug or a teacup is the perfect starting project! There is something incredibly satisfying about sipping a warm drink from a vessel you literally gathered from the local earth.

Since you are working with wild, hand-processed clay, making a functional mug involves a couple of fun structural challenges to keep in mind as you sculpt:

1. Building the Body (The Pinch or Coil Method)

Without a potter's wheel, you have two excellent traditional options:

  • The Pinch Pot: Start with a smooth ball of clay, press your thumb down into the center (leaving about a half-inch at the bottom), and gently pinch the walls upward and outward in a circle until the walls are uniform.
  • Coil Building: Roll out long, pencil-thick "snakes" of clay and layer them upward in a circle, scratching and wetting the clay between layers (called scoring and slipping) to weld them together, then smoothing out the ridges.

2. The Golden Rule of Mug Handles

If you add a handle, remember that wild clay shrinks significantly as it dries and fires (often up to 10% to 15%).

  • Because the handle is thin and exposed to the air on all sides, it dries much faster than the thick body of the mug. If it dries too fast, it will pull away and snap off before it even touches a fire.
  • The Fix: Once your mug is assembled, cover it loosely with a plastic bag to slow down the evaporation. You want the handle and the cup body to dry at the exact same speed.

3. Testing Your Blue Clay's "Mature" Temperature

Every wild clay has a different melting point depending on the minerals inside it. Because your clay is blue-purple, it likely has a decent amount of iron.

  • Iron acts as a flux, meaning it lowers the melting point of clay.
  • Before you fire your final, beautiful teacup, it is always a good idea to roll out a tiny, flat "test tile" of your processed clay and fire that first. You want to make sure the clay bakes into a hard ceramic rather than melting into a glassy puddle if it gets too hot!

turns.prompt_text: I wonder if there's anything I could add into the clay to make it closer to the ceramic I buy at Walmart for dishes
turns.response_html:
To get that smooth, glassy, and completely waterproof quality of commercial dishes (like stoneware or porcelain), you have to change the basic chemistry of your wild clay.

The dishes you buy at a store are vitrified, meaning they were fired hot enough that the silica inside the clay literally melted into a dense, non-porous glass. Most raw river or ravine clays are earthenware—if you fire them too hot to try and turn them into glass, the high iron content acts as a trigger and causes them to completely melt into a bloated, deformed puddle on the kiln shelf.

Commercial manufacturers achieve that high-quality finish by building a triaxial blend. They combine three core raw materials in precise ratios:

The Magic Trio

If you want to turn your blue ravine clay into something closer to factory-strength stoneware, you can buy these raw mineral powders online or at a local pottery supply shop and wedge them into your processed wet clay:

  1. Your Wild Clay (The Plastic Base): ~50% to 60% This provides the structural "glue" and flexibility needed to shape the teacup.
  2. Feldspar (The Flux): ~20% to 25% Feldspar is a mineral powder that acts like a catalyst. It dramatically lowers the melting point of the silica in your clay. It allows the clay body to fuse into a dense, rock-hard glass matrix at achievable kiln temperatures without the whole cup collapsing.
  3. Flint/Silica (The Glass-Former): ~15% to 20% Adding pure, fine ground silica gives the feldspar more material to turn into glass. It also strengthens the fired piece and prevents your glazes from cracking or crazing later on.

Making It Safe for Food and Drinks

While adding those minerals makes the clay physically match commercial dishes, vitrification and glaze are what make it safe to drink out of.

  • The Microscopic Trap: Raw fired earthenware is like a hard sponge; it absorbs water. If you drink coffee out of raw, unglazed wild clay, liquid will seep into the microscopic pores. Over time, bacteria will grow inside the walls of the mug, making it unsafe to reuse.
  • The Seal: To make your wild clay teacup 100% food-safe, it must be coated in a high-quality, commercial, lead-free glaze and fired to its mature temperature. The glaze acts as a continuous sheet of protective glass that seals off those porous clay walls completely.

The Best Next Step

Since you have that great blue clay ready to process, the absolute best thing you can do is make a few tiny, flat test tiles (about the size of a couple of stacked poker chips) out of your pure wild clay.

Take them to a local ceramics studio or an art department and ask to slip them into a low-fire (Cone 06) or mid-fire (Cone 6) kiln. Seeing how your specific ravine clay responds to the heat completely raw will tell you exactly how much feldspar or silica you need to add to reach that perfect Walmart-dish density!

But if I could do this it would make it really cost effective for me to be able to make custom dishes and cookware, assuming I am able to dishwash it or hand wash it
turns.response_html:
It absolutely requires a healthy dose of patience and a bit of a mad-scientist mentality, but it is an incredibly practical, rewarding way to get custom pieces. People have been doing it for millennia, and with a little modern testing, you can definitely make it dishwasher- and hand-wash-safe.

The big payoff is that once you dial in the right formula for your specific ravine clay, you have a virtually infinite, free supply of a custom material that nobody else has.

The Realities of Modern Use (Dishwasher vs. Hand Wash)

To make your custom dishes survive a modern kitchen, your focus will be entirely on two things: vitrification and glaze fit.

  • The Dishwasher Test: Dishwashers are brutal on ceramics. They use incredibly high heat, intense water pressure, and harsh, abrasive detergents.
  • The Porosity Problem: If your wild clay isn't fired hot enough to fuse completely (vitrify), or if you use a formulation without enough flux/silica, the clay inside remains slightly porous. In the dishwasher, water will force its way into the clay body beneath the glaze. When it heats up and expands, it can cause the glaze to web crack (crazing), pop off (shivering), or eventually split the handle right off your mug.
  • The Hand Wash Alternative: If your early test batches end up firing beautifully but remain slightly porous (common with low-fire wild earthenware), they are perfect for hand-washing! You just wash them with normal soap, rinse, and let them air-dry completely so moisture doesn't get trapped.

Shortcutting the Learning Curve

Getting the formula right does take trial and error, but you don't have to guess in isolation.

Since you are right there in Ames, you have an incredible resource nearby: The Workspace at the Iowa State Memorial Union. They have a fully functioning clay studio with programmable electric kilns and open studio hours.

Instead of trying to build a backyard pit fire (which won't get hot enough to vitrify dishes to modern "Walmart-strength" standards), you can process your blue clay, roll out a few small test tiles, and look into using a local community kiln or studio to test fire them.

Seeing exactly how that dark purple-blue ravine clay reacts to standard kiln temperatures ($Cone\ 06$ or $Cone\ 6$) will give you the exact baseline you need to know what minerals to add for a perfect, dishwasher-safe dish set.
